problems.description: Cognitive complexity +55 (per SonarQube) driven by the added guard-clause validation in edit_task/add_task; acceptable since they are flat early-returns, but the PUT handler could be factored into a validate_payload helper to keep the route thin.
Module-level init_db() call executes a side effect (schema creation) on import; justified for WSGI/test compat and idempotent, but worth noting as an import-time side effect.

Static convention score (0.71, 8 violations) is dominated by pre-existing issues in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py PascalCase/UPPER_CASE warnings). No violations are actually introduced by the changed lines.

strengths: Removes dead code: _legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task, and stale section-comment noise, reducing smells by 3 with no duplication added.
Fixes a real correctness bug — new tasks were inserted with status 'done' instead of 'pending'.
Replaces deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc).
Adds a solid pytest suite (7 tests) covering default status, input validation, ordering, and 404 paths.
Tightens request validation on PUT (non-dict bodies, missing fields, non-empty title, typed status) matching the added tests.
Keeps the single-file Flask structure, existing get_db()/get_tasks() helpers, and API surface intact, preserving the baseline seams.
commit_reviews.summary: A disciplined cleanup commit that removes dead code, fixes the default-status bug, and adds real test coverage while fully respecting the existing single-file Flask architecture — the low static convention score is contaminated by pre-existing violations in untouched files, not by this change.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT: manual base64url encoding, HMAC signing and token parsing in app.py instead of a vetted library (PyJWT). Roll-your-own-crypto risk, especially the manual header/payload/signature split and validation.

Insecure default secret: `JWT_SECRET` falls back to the literal "development-secret-change-me", so any deployment missing the env var issues forgeable tokens. Should fail hard or generate a per-process secret.
+27 cognitive complexity (SonarQube) concentrated in get_current_user: dense inline validation with nested try/except, header equality check, exp/sub type checks and a subquery all in one function.
No tests added for the new auth flow (register, login, token validation, owner scoping) despite the diff touching security-sensitive logic.
Regression in typing: original public functions had hints (`def create_task(title: str) -> dict`); rewritten signatures (create_task, get_task, update_task, register, login) drop them.
Long single-line expressions (header/payload construction, `f"{header}.{payload}.{signature}"` string building) exceed typical line lengths.

strengths: Uses hmac.compare_digest for constant-time signature comparison
Password storage via werkzeug generate_password_hash (proper hashing)
Schema migration via PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE preserves existing task rows
Owner scoping (`WHERE owner_id = ?`) on every task query prevents cross-user access
commit_reviews.summary: Discrepancy flagged: the 8 convention violations reference files outside this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) and the app.py class/PascalCase items appear spurious for a file that defines only snake_case functions, so the 0.71 score reflects pre-existing codebase state rather than this commit; the commit adds a coherent, owner-scoped auth feature but introduces real technical debt via hand-rolled JWT, an insecure default secret, dropped type hints, and no test coverage, making it a net-neutral change.

problems.description: Notification is enqueued after update_task commits but .delay() has no error handling: if the broker is down the request 500s while the task is already marked completed, and since the transition is then gone a retry will never re-trigger — the notification is silently lost.
Non-atomic check-then-act: previous_task is fetched via a separate get_task call before update_task, so a concurrent edit could enqueue based on stale state or miss the transition.
g.user['username'] is passed as the user_email parameter to send_notification_email — the name mismatch makes the intended recipient ambiguous (username is not an email address).

Mechanical convention score (0.71) is overstated: all 8 flagged violations are analyzer false positives (e.g. Flask/Celery app-instance variables flagged as classes/constants) or pre-existing in files this commit never touches (repositories.py is absent from the diff).

strengths: Transition-only guard is correct: re-putting status 'completed' or renaming does not re-notify, and a dedicated test locks this in.
Clean separation of concerns: celery_config.py owns wiring, tasks.py owns job definitions, app.py only orchestrates the enqueue.
Explicit Celery task name and route to a dedicated 'notifications' queue follow operational conventions.
Tests monkeypatch .delay() following existing patterns, so the suite runs without a broker.
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally sound async notification feature with correct transition gating and clean module separation, but enqueue-after-commit without broker-failure handling risks silent notification loss; qualitative convention adherence is higher than the mechanical 0.71, which is inflated by analyzer false positives and pre-existing violations in untouched repositories.py.

problems.description: BaseRepository._repository_contract is a stub abstract method returning None, used only to force the ABC to be abstract; it adds cognitive complexity (+12) with no behavior. Prefer a real abstract method or drop the ABC.
Repositories take get_db (Flask g-context) as a connection_factory callable, coupling the data layer to Flask's request context; a context manager/proxy would decouple it more cleanly.
New TaskRepository/UserRepository and initialize_database are untested; unit tests for the repository layer would lock in the refactor.

Mechanical convention score of 0.71 is dominated by pre-existing violations in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py); the new repositories.py itself follows snake_case methods / PascalCase classes.

strengths: Preserves owner_id scoping on all task queries, retaining the existing authorization boundary
Centralizes schema creation/migration into initialize_database, removing duplicated SQL from app.py
Reduces duplication and smells (smells -6, duplications 0.0%) while introducing no new bugs
Reuses the existing context-managed get_db() connection pattern rather than inventing a new one
New file follows project conventions (PascalCase classes, snake_case methods, type-hinted public surface)
commit_reviews.summary: A sound repository-layer extraction that preserves security scoping and the existing connection pattern while cutting duplication, with only minor seams (stub abstract method, Flask-context coupling) worth tightening.

problems.description: flask_limiter is instantiated with the deprecated `Limiter(app=app)` constructor arg (v3 deprecates this in favor of `Limiter(key_func=...)` + `limiter.init_app(app)`); will break on upgrade.

Pagination protocol (limit+1 overfetch, has_next_page, next_cursor) is computed in the route handler while `get_tasks` remains a thin wrapper — pagination policy leaks into the transport layer instead of the repository/service layer.

`TaskRepository(get_db())` is instantiated twice inside list_tasks (once via get_tasks, once inline for count_for_owner); a `count_tasks` helper at the same layer as get_tasks would be more consistent.
`total` runs a COUNT(*) query on every page, which is O(n) and unbounded as the table grows; the count is not needed for cursor-based navigation.
Ordering silently changed from `ORDER BY created_at DESC` to `ORDER BY id DESC` to enable keyset pagination; correlated for autoincrement ids but a semantic behavior change not called out.

Measured convention score 0.71 (8 violations) reflects pre-existing issues in celery_config.py and tasks.py, which are NOT touched by this diff; the commit's own additions (rate_limit_key, count_for_owner, REDIS_URL, Limiter) are all snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE compliant.

strengths: Rate limiting is scoped per authenticated user via get_current_user() with a remote_addr fallback, plus headers_enabled=True and Retry-After — a good fit for the auth model.
Cursor pagination is correct for a DESC keyset: next_cursor derived from the last row's id, limit+1 overfetch, and a proper next_cursor=None terminal state.
Input validation rejects limit/cursor that are non-positive or limit > 100 with a clear 400 message and a dedicated parametrized test.
SQL uses bound `?` params throughout despite the f-string construction — no injection risk.
New tests cover pagination ordering, invalid params, and 429 rate limiting; the fixture calls task_app.limiter.reset() and existing tests were updated for the new response shape.
REDIS_URL follows the existing DATABASE/JWT_SECRET env-var pattern with a sane default and in-memory fallback for resilience.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid feature commit (per-user rate limiting + cursor pagination) that fits the repository/env-var patterns and ships good tests, but the deprecated flask_limiter `app=` API and page-level COUNT add mild debt, and the 0.71 convention score stems from pre-existing violations in files outside this diff.

compounding_issues: No requirements.txt existed until Session 5, so dependency/env issues (pytest not on PATH, missing runtime deps) recurred in Sessions 1 and 4
Session 2 hand-rolled an HMAC JWT codec instead of using a library; every later session was constrained to work within that custom token format and the same JWT_SECRET/JWT_LIFETIME constants
The users schema stores only a username with no email field, forcing Session 3 to use the username as the notification email address — a placeholder that persists through the final commit
Session 4's refactor accidentally committed runtime artifacts (__pycache__/, todos.db) alongside repositories.py
The BaseRepository._repository_contract abstract method is a no-op placeholder, and generic CRUD uses f-string interpolated column names (SQL-injection smell if columns were ever user-controlled)
key_decisions: Session 1: fixed the seed's inverted default status ('done'->'pending'), made init_db run on import, added request validation and UTC-aware timestamps
Session 2: added JWT auth with an idempotent SQLite migration (PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE for owner_id) and owner-scoped queries — the ownership model every later session builds on
Session 3: integrated Redis-backed Celery for async completion notifications, triggered on the status transition to 'completed'
Session 4: extracted a repository layer (BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository), moving all SQL out of app.py while preserving behavior
Session 5: added Redis-backed Flask-Limiter with in-memory fallback for testability, plus cursor-based pagination over task IDs and a first dependency manifest
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the five sessions. The story follows a textbook escalation — greenfield cleanup, then a feature (auth), then integration (Celery), then refactor (repository layer), then cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, pagination, packaging) — with each session building directly on the prior one. Test coverage grew from 8 to 18 passing tests with no regression: the Session 4 refactor was behavior-preserving (tests stayed green), and Session 5 extended the existing auth, ownership, and repository structure rather than reworking it. The architecture tightened from a single-file Flask app with a few leftover seed stubs to a cleanly modular codebase (app, repositories, tasks, celery_config, requirements.txt) with strong validation, migration, and security handling.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, well-tempered progression in which each session layered naturally onto the last — fixing, extending, integrating, refactoring, and hardening a small Flask API — with quality and test coverage rising steadily to a clean, fully-tested 18-pass final state.
